short: A versatile British combat aircraft constructed almost entirely of wood, renowned for its extraordinary speed and range.
full:
Introduced in 1941, the de Havilland Mosquito was a remarkably unorthodox twin-engine combat aircraft constructed primarily from plywood and balsa wood. Originally conceived as an unarmed fast bomber, its aerodynamic purity and powerful Merlin engines made it faster than most dedicated single-seat fighters of the era. Its wooden construction conserved critical strategic metals and allowed production to be dispersed to furniture factories and cabinet makers across Britain and the Commonwealth.

The Mosquito proved astonishingly versatile, excelling in roles its designers never anticipated. It served as a pathfinder, a night fighter equipped with radar, a low-level strike aircraft, and an ultra-long-range photo-reconnaissance platform. Operating often without defensive armament and relying purely on speed to evade interception, it suffered among the lowest loss rates of any aircraft in Bomber Command, remaining in service well into the 1950s.
